    • Optimize comp works on any comp: a ContactSheet whose grid comes from its inputs, or a control set apart for each view, stopped the measuring (MM1_050, RAI_360). Such nodes copy, paste and undo as they are now; anything that still can't be copied is left out of the times and named under them.

    New

    • The manual opens with Kento and NukeX side by side: every result of the 14 Nov speed tests on the studio's comps, the losses with the wins, and how they were measured.
    • Help > Kento manual is easier to read and search: Back and Forward, a narrower reading column with Smaller and Larger text, On this page beside it, Node Reference chapters that open to their nodes, and a search that finds the right place (a node, a section, a control) with a line of its text, from the keyboard.
    • Optimize comp finds grain that isn't last: a grain node or gizmo (Grain, ScannedGrain, DasGrain, the regrain plug-in) with merges, grades or a TimeBlur after it. Move grain to the end puts it just before the Reformat, Crop or Write that finish the picture, timed both ways first; Keep as it is leaves it. Where a keyer or a mask reads the grained picture it says why it can't move.
    • A merge with A2, A3 and more, or a MultiMerge with several layer masks, grows taller in the Node Graph so every input on its side sits on its edge, evenly spaced, each name rising on the diagonal from its own wire, level with its input; it stays where it was, and a merge with only A and B looks as before.
    • A node with many inputs on top (a Switch with eleven or twenty, a MultiMerge with sixteen) widens in the Node Graph so every input sits over it, evenly spaced, with its name in the middle; it stays where it was, and a node with a few inputs looks as before.
    • Input names on the Node Graph rise on the diagonal from their ports, so a node with many inputs (Kiri's five, a Merge's A2 and up, ScanlineRender's bg, obj/scn and cam) shows every name clear of the others and of the wires; single letters and digits (A, B, 1) stay level.
    • Optimize comp suggests faster Kento nodes for a comp from Nuke: an IDefocus gizmo becomes Kento's Map Defocus, a TimeBlur below a moving Transform becomes the Transform's own motion blur. Each is timed both ways on a copy and listed only when faster, with how much the picture changes; Keep matching Nuke leaves it as it is. Also the studio's HighlightSuppress group becomes one Expression, with its mask and mix (the same picture within rounding); KeymixBBox groups are checked as Kento's Keymix too (the same picture), but they only show when that is faster.
    • MultiMerge: each layer has its own mask and transform. Click a layer's row and its mask (the layer itself or its own mask input, any channel, invert) and its translate, rotate, scale and center show under the list, with its handle in the Viewer; a layer's mask port shows on the tile only while it uses one. The node's own mask and mix work on the whole stack, as on other nodes.
    • The studio's own lens database: the Lens node's lens picker (now called Lenses) lists the lenses the studio has measured first, and opens on the one the plate's metadata names, with each focus distance it was measured at.
    • Add a lens from a grid, in the Lenses window: solve a lens from images of a checkerboard shot through it and save it to the studio's lenses.
    • Lenses travel between Kentos as small lens files: Export lens and Import lens in the Lenses window (or drop a .kentolens file on it or on the Lens panel), and Export as Lensfun XML for other tools.
    • Save to the studio, on the Lens panel: keeps the Lens's own lens, with the plate's lens metadata, in the studio's lens database for every show.
    • Settings > Files and paths > Studio lenses: says how many studio lenses this Mac has and where they came from, sets the folder they come from (the studio library, or a project drive or folder of your own), and Copy the studio lenses here... writes them into a folder for a Kento that can't see the library.
    • The studio's lens database now holds the Cheetos zoom's on-set grids, decoded with ARRI's own decoder, beside its matchmove solves (on probation until their corners are measured).

    Faster

    • A wide Median (size 4 and up) takes about a third less time, the same to the bit.
    • MotionBlur no longer spends seconds a frame checking whether its neighboring frames are held: a comp with a MotionBlur on a 4K plate prepares each frame in 1.7 s instead of 4.6 s.
    • A masked node works out only what its mask's box reaches: a comp with a wide Median under a small roto renders more than twice as fast (5.9 to 2.6 s a frame on the Mac Studio, 15.3 to 5.9 s on a 16 GB Mac).
    • Command-line renders work out a frame's next Writes while the current one renders, and a still picture (a PNG or Photoshop file read on every frame) is decoded once and shared, not copied each frame: a fifth to a quarter less time a frame on comps with several Writes.
    • Reads in a comp that uses Nuke's own color management (clamped before their LUT) and one-channel pictures read into red render in Kento's engine again, instead of falling back to the slower path.
    • A command-line render of frames far apart decodes a movie a few frames around each one, not 24 frames at a time: with the Reads above, two studio comps with movies render about three times as fast on such frames (14.5 to 4.4 s a frame on the Mac Studio).
    • Each Write's time in a command-line render's log is its own: a light Write next to a heavy one was charged the heavy one's setup (a plate Write read 0.39 s a frame, 0.18 s now).
    • ZDefocus and Bokeh run on the GPU on a Mac: in a 4K frame on a 16 GB Mac the depth defocus takes about a third less time and the frame about a fifth less CPU (within a millionth of the CPU's picture).
    • Dragging a control is quicker: a Grade's gain slider takes about a third of the time a step it did with its Properties open (about 25 to 8 ms on a small comp, 59 to 26 on a 500-node shot), and moving an object by its handle in the 3D view about a fifth less (31 to 25 ms). While you drag, the key values under the node in the Node Graph follow a few times a second instead of every step.
    • Median runs on the GPU on a Mac, with the same picture as before: a size 14 Median over a 4K matte takes about a tenth of a second on a 16 GB Mac instead of over a second and a half.
    • Convolve runs on the GPU on a Mac, for any size of filter and any brightness of picture: a 161 pixel disc on a 4K picture takes under a fifth of a second on a 16 GB Mac instead of seven and a half, and a 41 pixel one about a quarter of the time. MM1_080 renders in 3.0 s instead of 3.6.
    • More of a 4K frame runs on the GPU on a Mac, without copying pictures to it: Colorspace (linear, gamma, rec709 and sRGB) and Transform's scales and moves. Merges with over, matte, stencil and the other formulas are faster too. On a 16 GB Mac, RAI_360 renders in 1.2 s instead of 2.2, RAI_220 in 3.0 instead of 3.9, BOU_180 in 2.8 instead of 3.3.
    • Erode (filter) runs on the GPU on a Mac: a 4K frame with a Gaussian grow of 200 renders about a sixth faster again on a 16 GB Mac (within a ten-millionth of the CPU's picture).

    • Long frame numbers, such as eight-digit timecode frames, show every digit in the Timeline's start, end and frame fields and the ruler's numbers no longer run into each other; the fields are sized with the range, so nothing on the line moves while it plays.
    • Clicking in the Viewer where a Roto shape is that isn't alive at this frame, or has its visibility off, no longer does nothing: a card says which shape and why ("Shape3 isn't alive at frame 1040", its life 1001 to 1030), with Extend its life to here or Make it visible as the fix.
    • A .nk comp on Nuke 17's ACES 2.0 configs (fn-nuke_cg-config-v3.0.0 and the studio one) uses that config, so its Reads' default color spaces (matte_paint, texture_paint, compositing_log) are the comp's own.
    • A one-channel picture (a gray PNG, TIFF or JPEG) reads into red and is converted like red, as the comp had it, instead of an unconverted other.Y.
    • LightKey's Screen PreBlur and the tuning gains (Shadow, Midtones and Highlights Gain, Mid Tones At) now work, Clip Rollback works (closely from 2 pixels up, roughly below), and Alpha Bias and Despill Bias key off-gray screens as the original does on a green screen.
    • LightKey's Source Alpha Handling now works: Normal keys only where the source's alpha is, and Add To Inside Mask adds the source's alpha to the inside mask (both had been taken as Ignore).

    Faster

    • The processing glow on the Node Graph steps more coarsely the bigger the comp, and on a comp too big to pulse without slowing the interface it glows steady instead.
    • Playback from a full cache keeps its pace: a 24 fps comp plays at 24, where it ran at about 18.
    • A big comp settles sooner after it opens: the menus are no longer built a second time (about 2 seconds on a large comp).
    • After a big comp opens, its Node Graph no longer redraws itself over and over (about a quarter as many redraws on an 11,000-node comp); only the processing glow pulses in coarser steps there.
    • Heavy 4K comps render faster, the same picture: a 3D scene of textured cards with motion blur about a quarter faster, and frames with Bokeh or LightKey about a fifth faster, on a 16 GB Mac.
    • Erode (filter) with a large size renders several times faster, the same picture: a 4K frame with a Gaussian grow of 200 renders a third faster on a 16 GB Mac.
    • Convolve renders about 25 times faster: a comp with a lens-defocus gizmo built on Convolve renders in minutes, where one shot took over 8 hours.
    • NoTimeBlur keeps a TimeBlur's sub-frames from everything above it, with any rounding: those nodes see the whole frame and are worked out once a frame, where they were sampled at each sub-frame (rounding none) or at two frames (floor, rint, ceil).
    • Convolve no longer darkens a plate toward its edges: past the input's box it repeats the edge pixels, where it read black (up to 0.32 off with a 41-pixel disc).
    • Comps with a TimeBlur render faster and in far less memory: parts of the comp that don't change between its sub-frames are worked out once (a whole shot in 18 minutes and 16 GB, where its last frame alone stalled for over 20 minutes).
    • Moving objects in the 3D view is smoother in every draw mode: a sphere's wireframe is no longer rebuilt and the comp's insides are no longer searched at each step of the drag. With the render shown in a Viewer beside it, the drag stays smooth too: the Viewer holds its picture while you drag, catches up when you pause, and shows the result when you let go (a step about 200 ms to 60-120 ms). Every Python expression also runs faster, compiled once instead of at every run.
    • MotionBlur works out its motion faster, the same picture: on a 16 GB Mac its motion vectors take about a quarter less time at 2K and a fifth less at 4K; VectorGenerator gains too.
    • VectorRetime renders about 40 percent faster at 4K and 30 percent at 2K on a 16 GB Mac, the same picture: its warps no longer carry the motion vectors along.
    • VectorGenerator with confidence on and VectorRetime with blend if unsure render in Kento's own render engine, the same picture as before.
    • Dragging an object in the 3D view is about twice as quick again (a step about 70 ms to 35 in Wire, 95 to 45 in Lit), with the Node Graph waiting until you pause. In Lit, the dragged object's surface now moves with it, where it stayed behind until you let go; Shaded, Textured and Lit draw at half detail while you drag and in full when you let go.
    • A big comp's window freezes less just after it opens: the Shot panel no longer holds it while it lists the shot (it says "Looking up the shot..." until the list comes), and its Node Graph redraws less in its first second; the longest freeze on a 16 GB Mac is about 0.7 seconds, where it was often over 1.
    • Bokeh and ZDefocus render their depth layers about a quarter faster, and a 3D scene of cards flattens faster, the same picture.

1.0.16 (build 5031)   Nov 18, 2026   This version

New

  • A new node, To ACEScg, in the Generative menu, brings generated video, web pictures and client stills into an ACEScg comp the right way. Pick what the image is in What is it?, with a line under the menu saying what each choice assumes: Generated video or web image (sRGB) (the right choice for most generated media), Video from a camera or edit (Rec.709), the Rec.709 camera curve for footage that really is scene light, Match the Viewer exactly so it shows as it did in a browser, Already linear Rec.709 and Already ACEScg. Guess from the file reads the movie's or picture's color tags and picks for you, saying why (a movie tagged Rec.709 that a video generator such as Seedance, Runway, Kling, Sora or Veo made is taken as sRGB, as generated video is), and sorts out a Read that was converting the file too. Alpha stays as it is. It runs through your comp's color config, or the same math built in when the config hasn't the spaces; the render engine does the same, it is saved with the comp, and a Nuke script gets a group of Nuke's own color nodes doing the same.
  • Nuke camera channel files (.chan) read and write. A Camera with a .chan file and Read from file keys its translate and rotate from the file, and its focal length from the vertical field of view column when the file has one; the Camera's own rotation order turns the numbers, as in Nuke. A Write Geo set to .chan writes the first camera in the scene, a line a frame with its translate, rotate and vertical field of view, and the file reads back as the same camera. Write Geo's file type menu has Camera channels (chan).
  • A Read's premultiplied works. Turn it on for a file whose color is already multiplied by its alpha (a premultiplied render, a ProRes 4444): the input transform divides the alpha out, converts the color, and multiplies it back, so the soft edges convert correctly. Off, the default, converts the values as they are. It is saved with the comp, read from a Nuke script, and the render engine does the same.

Improved

  • The color space menus are short now. A Read's input transform (and a Write's output transform, a Colorspace node's in and out, and the menu behind a Read's tag in the Node Graph) lists default, the comp's working space and the common spaces first: ACEScg, ACES2065-1, Linear Rec.709, sRGB, Rec.709, the Gamma ones, ARRI LogC3 and LogC4, S-Log3, Log3G10, V-Log, CanonLog3, Blackmagic Film Gen 5, DaVinci Intermediate and Raw, by the names your config gives them. The last five you chose are under Recent. Every other space is in a submenu for its family (Input, then ARRI, Sony or RED; Utility; ACES), with Other for spaces without one and Display for the display spaces. Type to find a space in any submenu. Comps and .nk files are unchanged.
  • A paused Viewer is easy to see now: while you have Pause updates on, its button turns solid red with a white icon, and the Paused chip in the Viewer's corner is solid red with white text. Both stay readable at every interface brightness.
  • A node's properties floated in a window of their own now look like the rest of Kento: the window is titled with the node's name, the panel fills it in Kento's dark look with no light gray frame, and it is as tall as its rows, with no empty strip under them. While a panel floats, the button in its header is Dock, which closes the window and puts the panel back at the top of the Properties bin.
  • A new workspace for cutting: Window > Workspaces > Edit puts the Viewer and Properties side by side across the top and the Dope Sheet across the whole width below them, already in Edit mode, with the Node Graph and Curve Editor as tabs beside it. The Compositing workspace is unchanged.

Fixed

  • A Viewer could show a black picture while everything behind it was right, with the Pause updates button lit and nothing saying it was paused. The button now shows only your own pause (not the pause the Viewer uses while it plays a held frame or while you drag in the 3D view), a paused Viewer shows a small Paused chip in its top right corner that un-pauses when you click it, and a Viewer paused before it has drawn anything draws one picture first and then holds it.
  • A movie in the Viewer at Half or Quarter (While playing, or a Viewer set to work smaller) showed in the wrong colors, a blue sky cyan and warm colors pink. It now looks the same at every size.
  • Edit mode's filmstrip showed a movie's frames in the same wrong colors. The frames now look as they do in the Viewer.
  • On a Read, premultiplied, raw data and auto alpha all showed gray as if they weren't built, and raw data and auto alpha couldn't be clicked in the panel (they shared a row with the not-yet premultiplied switch). The three are working switches on one row now. Raw data and auto alpha themselves were already right; note that a movie's pictures already have an alpha of 1, so auto alpha changes nothing on a movie.
  • The charts in the Utility menu (Color checker, Grey card, Color bars, Color wheel) made a node with no input or output. Each now shows its output port, wires into a Viewer or a Merge, draws its chart at the comp's format, and goes under the selected node as a node made with Tab does. Its panel says what it is (the checker lists its 24 patches by name), and it saves and opens again in a .ko or .nk. Any group made empty and given its output afterward shows its ports now too.

Earlier updates

1.0.15 (build 4995)   Nov 18, 2026

New

  • A working resolution: Kento works the comp out at the size your screen can show while you work, and at full when you stop. Settings, Performance, Working resolution sets it for every Viewer: While you work (Auto, Full, Half or Quarter), While playing, While dragging a control, and When you stop (Full or Stay). Auto picks the smallest size that still fills the Viewer's real pixels, so a 4K plate in a Viewer on a 1x display works at Half, and on a Retina display at Full; when it picks a smaller size, a small card by the Viewer says so and fades. Stopped for a couple of seconds, the frame comes back at full. Renders and Writes are always full resolution. The Viewer's two Downscale menus are now one control on bar 2, with Auto, the sizes (Nuke's 1:2 and 1:4 beside them), While playing and Full resolution when stopped, and a chip in the Viewer's corner says the size it is working at. Settings, Performance opens with what Kento suggests for this Mac (from its memory, GPU, display and cache drive), with Use these and Keep mine, and a card says what was picked the first time Kento starts on a Mac. The disk cache keeps the Viewers' results as compressed half float (about a fifth of the size), depth and other data as full float, at the working size by default on a 16 GB Mac (Keep results at: Working size, Full size or Both side by side), is on by default on every Mac, and a frame you leave never waits for its results to be read back. Renders keep and read full-precision results only.
  • The Dope Sheet has an Edit mode. Click Edit at the start of its strip, beside Keys and Footage, and the comp's clips (Reads, TimeClips, AppendClips, a clip laid over a Merge) show as tracks, as an editor shows a cut. Trim where you point, as in an editor's trim mode: just left of a join ripples the clip's end, on the join rolls it, just right of it ripples the next clip's start, the upper half of a clip slips its frames and the lower half slides it between its neighbors. A chip names the trim as the pointer arrives. While you drag, a tag says what it does and what it snaps to, and the Viewer shows the frame before the edit and the frame after it side by side; let go and it is one undo. Cut at the playhead, change a clip's speed, reverse it, hold a frame, dissolve the joins (from each clip's handles, a red end where a clip has no more frames) and delete a clip closing the gap. Each clip keeps a history to go back to a step (Settings, Node Graph, Keep clip history). The keys are an editor's own (A, T, W, B, N, Shift+Cmd+L and the rest, listed in Settings, Shortcuts) and Keys mode keeps its own. Everything is written to the comp's own clip nodes, so the comp renders what you see, and a Nuke script keeps the trims, cuts, speeds and dissolves. A show's cut on a Cut node, snapshots, proxies while playing and comps on segments come later and show dim with what brings them.
  • Edit mode's clips know their versions. A clip whose file name has a version (v001, _v12) shows a chip saying which one plays and how many are on disk (v001 of 3), with a dot when a newer one has been written. Control+Option+Up and Control+Option+Down step the picked clips to the next version and the one before, Shift+Option+Up to the latest; click the chip for the list, with when each was made and by whom where known. A swap keeps the cut as it was, the same frames in the same places, and is one undo. A version that lacks frames the cut uses isn't swapped: a card by the clip says which frames are missing and offers Trim to fit or Keep the length. A clip can follow the latest version, taking each new one by itself with a Back on its notice; new clips stay on the version they came in with. All clips to their latest version updates the picked clips, or the whole timeline, in one undo and says what changed. Browse for a version takes any file, from another app or a vendor, marked external on the chip and kept in the clip's menu. Versions are found in the background, so a slow drive never holds up the edit.
  • Edit mode can take a version before all its frames are on disk. Wait for the frames keeps the clip's length and every frame in its place; frames that aren't there yet show a dark hatched picture naming the version and the frames ("Frames not on disk yet: v004, 1013 to 1016"), never black, and are hatched on the track, filling in by themselves as the files land. A clip following the latest version now takes a newer one this way even when it is short, and its card says which frames are still to come. Refresh this version (Control+Option+R) and Refresh all versions (Shift+Control+Option+R) read the files again, for a version picked up before its render finished. All clips to their latest version keeps external picks, and its card offers Move external picks too; the version menu has both. Trim a clip into a gap beside it, or ripple a gap shorter. With sync lock on, a track running across an edit that ripples gets a gap opened in it, or the same frames taken out, so what comes after stays in step. Their colorspace is still unchecked, and so are Luma AI's (its sample stood up Y down but tipped) and DJI Terra's (no sample yet).
  • ColorCurves spares grays better. A new ColorCurves fades its hue curves toward gray with a steeper shape at 0.06 (the spare grays row's new Steep fade), so the grain on a gray wall or a white car takes far less of a hue turn (about 2 degrees of a 20 degree turn, was about 9, measured on 10 studio plates) while pale colors such as skin in shade still take most of it. ColorCurves nodes in comps saved before open with the Gentle fade they had and look exactly as they did; choose Steep and 0.06 to give one the new fade.
  • The Node Graph stays readable at every interface brightness. Wires, ports and grid dots now lift with the ground, and the small words under the tiles get lighter as the tiles do: at brightness 30 wires are 4.5:1 on the ground (were 3:1) and the words 4.5:1 on every tile (were 3.1:1). Dark looks exactly as before.
  • Going back to a frame you have just looked at is now close to instant on a 16 GB Mac. The Viewer keeps the last frames it showed, in a part of the image cache set aside for them (half the render engine's share, so the total memory is the same). On a heavy 4K studio comp on a 16 GB Mac mini, a frame seen again took 7.6 seconds, as long as a new one; it now takes about 0.7. On a bigger Mac, 1.3 seconds became 0.65.
  • Motion blur on a moving Transform (a match move, for instance) is now added up on the GPU in one pass, with the same pixels as before. On a studio comp whose match move blurs 24 copies of a 4K plate, that part of a frame took 1.7 to 3.7 seconds on a 16 GB Mac mini and now takes about 0.3; a new frame in the Viewer went from 6.9 to 5.1 seconds.
  • The first frame of a comp with a learned model shows sooner. Most of its extra time was spent working out the model's input picture the slow way, a node at a time; that picture now comes from Kento's render engine, and only the channels the model reads. On a studio comp with DepthAnythingV2, the first picture after opening took 18 to 22 seconds on a 16 GB Mac mini and now takes 12 to 14; on a Mac Studio, 10 seconds became 6. Moving to another frame while the model is still running no longer waits for the model to finish.
  • Comps with a learned model (an Inference node, inside gizmos such as DepthAnythingV2) do less work at each new frame. Kento checked whether the model's input picture had changed once for every processor thread, up to 30 times a frame; it now checks once. On a heavy studio comp that is about 20 seconds less processor time a frame spent checking.
  • Furea's lens readout, LensDefocus's kernel preview, Roto's shape outlines and PixelKernel's kernel check no longer pause the rest of the interface while they work.

Fixed

  • A Flipbook made "As the Viewer shows it" with a cache node no longer hands its smaller frames to renders. Those frames are worked out at the Viewer's downscale, and a render through the cache node read them as if they were full size, so the render came out soft. The cache node now keeps the size each frame was made at: the Viewer at that downscale plays them, and a render, or the Viewer at full size, works the picture out at full size instead. Render out of date on the node makes them again at full size. After the comp is closed and opened again, an edit above the cache node still drops the frames it changes.
  • A file rewritten in place within the same second and at the same size (a quick re-render of an uncompressed DPX or EXR) is read again by renders and in the next session. Kento told a file's versions apart by its time to the second; it now uses the time to the nanosecond and the size, for the engine's results in memory and on disk, its file reads, decoded stills, layered files and movies, Edit mode's pictures and the proof sheet's copies. Decoded movies and stills are made once more after updating. A Viewer already showing the file still needs Reload, as before.
  • The Viewer no longer stays at Updating for minutes on a heavy comp. While the Viewer's picture caught up with a pan, a zoom or a window settling, the tiles it hadn't reached yet were worked out the slow way, a node at a time; on a heavy studio comp's car merge one tile took a minute, the Viewer said Updating for ten, and the interface stopped answering meanwhile. Those tiles now come from Kento's render engine too: the picture is there in about two seconds.
  • SmartMerge's Measure no longer stops the interface. It reads the shot in the background: the row says it's reading, with Cancel, and you can go on working; the numbers come in as one undo. Measure the defocus reads in the background too. SmartMerge and Levels read the plate and the element through Kento's render engine, so Measure on a heavy studio comp's car merge takes about 8 seconds for five frames (it froze the app for about ten minutes).
  • SmartMerge's read region follows a drag. The plate and the element are read once, then each change of the read menu, the band's width or the box is worked out in a fraction of a second, so the outline follows the band's square as you drag it. While the plate is read again (another frame, an upstream change) the last outline stays in the Viewer and its chip says it's reading.
  • The pick-whip's dotted line is drawn over Kento's own windows only. Before, it was drawn in a window the size of the screen that stayed above every app, and if a drag hung it stayed up over other apps too. It also goes away by itself once the drag is over.
  • ColorLookup's Adjust in Viewer moves the curve at a gentler pace: a stop for every 100 pixels you drag while the graph is shown in stops, and the curve's whole 0 to 1 over 400 pixels when it is shown 0 to 1 (Option still a tenth of that). Before, a short drag could move a gray to more than twice its value. A key dragged above the curve's last key no longer makes the curve fall below 0 past it, which had put colored streaks in bright highlights.
  • Adjust in Viewer (ColorLookup, HueCorrect) lets go when another node's panel opens above its own. Before, it stayed armed over the other node's picture, and a drag there made an undo step that changed nothing.
  • Clicking a node whose panel isn't open now scrolls the Properties bin to its panel. Before, the panel opened at the top while the bin stayed scrolled down, out of sight.
  • A node's name in the Node Graph stays inside its tile between 45% and 100% zoom: on two lines split where a word starts (Multi and Merge1, Color and Correct1) when one doesn't hold it, or whole under the tile when that doesn't work (Transform1 at about 50%, as further out). Before, MultiMerge1 and other names ran past the tile's end, under its right-hand port, at 50 to 66%.
  • Kento's splash at launch no longer floats over other apps: it shows over Kento only, and hides while you're in another app. Before, during a slow start it sat in the middle of the screen above every app and took clicks meant for them.
  • A ProofSheet's labels are drawn only while the Viewer shows the sheet, not over other nodes' pictures while its panel is open.
  • A wire dropped on a ProofSheet's tile goes to its next free input instead of replacing the first one.
  • Kento's assistant and Kento's other online services can connect again. With a hosted service (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or another https address), Settings' Test said Not reached even with a good key, and the assistant couldn't talk to it; the Hugging Face model list and the Shot panel's upload of a review movie failed the same way. They now connect through the system's own secure connection, and your API key is never shown to other programs on the computer. When a service turns a key down, Test now says Key refused, with the service's reason in its tooltip.
  • Settings' Test for Kento's assistant now says Key refused when a service turns your key down, even if it listed its models for you before. It used to show the old list's count, as if the key worked. The old list is still shown when the service can't be reached at all.
  • Your assistant API key and Kento's seat are no longer visible to other programs on the computer while Kento saves the key in the Mac's keychain or downloads LearnedLens's network or Kiri's MEMatte weights. Before, each was briefly in a system tool's command line, where any program listing the running processes could read it.
  • On the Mac, holding Control before you press on a node and dragging now takes the node out of its chain, as the manual says. Before, the Mac treated the press as a Control-click and opened the node's menu, and only Control pressed after the drag began worked. A Control-click that doesn't move still opens the menu.
  • Starting a wire on a large comp stays quick: whether each input would make a loop is worked out in one pass for the whole drag.
  • A wire that would make a loop now looks refused while you drag it, as a wire of the wrong kind does: the input fades, the loose end turns amber and struck through over it with the reason under the pointer, and letting go there shows a card saying why. Before, the input lit as if it would take the wire and the refusal said nothing. This works for new wires and for wires you pick up.
  • A ProofSheet cell you see alone in the Viewer (or scrub with its time bar) is now only how the Viewer shows it: a Write rendered at the same time, the render queue and a saved comp get the whole sheet. Before, a Write rendered while a cell was soloed rendered that one cell.
  • An AppendClip, ContactSheet or other node whose inputs grow as you wire them no longer prints an error each time it is rewired after its last inputs were disconnected.
  • A node that fails, such as a Read whose file is missing, no longer shows a red warning triangle half hidden behind its tile in the Node Graph, nor on the nodes and Dots below it. The failed node keeps its red edge and mark, a Read says "No picture", and its error card says what went wrong. Zoomed far out, the red edge no longer thins to nothing, so a failed node still shows.
  • A Grade with blackpoint equal to whitepoint now makes a hard step at that point, as Nuke's does. It used to pass the values through without a step. Comps that use this to turn any value above a point into a solid matte (a Grade on alpha with whitepoint 0, say) now look as they do in Nuke, so a Kento comp with such a Grade renders differently from before.
  • SmartMerge's color from a neutral picked in A now reads the place you picked. It read the same spot mirrored top to bottom, so a neutral picked high in A was read low in A.
  • RemoveGlare's glare fitted to a light now matches full size at a Viewer's 1:2 and 1:4 (and in the comp's proxy). At a smaller scale the fit measured the light in the smaller frame's own pixels, so it started and ended in other places and came out flatter: on the 10 studio plates where a light was fitted, the picture at 1:4 was 6.5% off full size on average and up to 20%. It now measures in full-size pixels: at 1:2 the picture matches full size, at 1:4 it is 0.7% off on average (one plate 5.9%, its falloff a step off). At 1:8, where the frame holds less of the light, it is 8% off on average (was 19%, up to 77%).
1.0.14 (build 4832)   Nov 17, 2026

New

  • A calmer Node Graph. Nothing on the graph moves, grows or appears unless you point at it: an input is named while the pointer is on it, and the selected node's wired inputs are named; the rest of the graph stays as it is. A computing node shows a yellow edge once it has worked for 0.4 seconds, and keeps its own color. Glows and flow chevrons are off by default (Settings > Node Graph).
  • One rule for inputs on every node: a node's main inputs always show (B and A on a merge, the first input elsewhere); every other input folds while nothing is wired to it into a small empty socket, with +2, +3 when there are more. Point at the node, or bring a wire near it, and they open in place. MultiMerge's mask inputs keep their own setting for now.
  • Pins and sockets: inputs are sockets and outputs are pins, and a wire ends in a ball seated in its input and starts in a cup round its output's pin, so the flow reads at either end. Pull a wire and its loose end is a ball; within about 28 pixels of an input that takes it, the ball jumps into the socket and the input is named, and letting go lands it exactly there, at any zoom. An input that won't take it leaves the ball outside, amber and struck through.
  • Easier to look at: six node families, each its own color and icon shape, lifted off the ground; brighter wires; long names on two lines instead of cut in the middle, and under the node when zoomed out; the words under nodes only where they can be read (from 75%, or on the selected node). A comp's graph opens with its wires already routed, a failed node keeps its red edge through an edit until it has computed again, and a plate that won't read shows "No picture" on its node.
  • Levels (Color menu): black, gray and white set on a histogram read in stops, so a scene-linear plate's shadows and sun each get room. Drag the histogram's handles or its Blacks, Mid-tones and Whites regions, type the values, or pick each From Viewer. Black and white say what they become (the white can instead keep its brightness, only made neutral). What's below 0, over the top, NaN or infinite is counted and never clamped. Option-drag a handle to see what it clips; Clipping in Viewer stripes it while you work.
  • Levels' Auto sets the ends, the ends and a neutral gray, or each channel's ends, then lists each thing it set and why, every line a switch, with Keep and Undo Auto. Presets by situation, with an amount.

  • ColorCurves (Color menu): every curve in one node, Tone (luma, red, green and blue) and Hue vs Hue, Hue vs Sat, Hue vs Lum, Lum vs Sat, Sat vs Sat and Sat vs Lum, worked out together in log and OKLCh with linear in and out. The picture's own spread sits behind each curve; curves never overshoot their points and hue wraps; values below 0 and above 1 pass through. Spare grays fades the hue curves out toward gray so neutral areas keep their color, and specular highlights keep their hue.
  • ColorCurves in the Viewer: press on a color and drag up or down to move the open curve there, click to add a point, Shift-drag to read an area; Neutral from Viewer, Blacks to..., and named markers shared with the Pixel inspector's pins.

An eye on each range turns it off (hold it to compare); presets with an amount (Split tone: teal and orange, Warm highlights, Cool shadows, Neutralize); Neutral from the Viewer takes a cast out with one click, and Shadows to... and Highlights to... give the picture's shadows or highlights the cast of the plate's, clicked in the Viewer. It grades in a log space, so it suits scene-linear plates, and runs on the GPU. A .nk gets a group with one Expression node doing the same sums.
  • Jump between keys. Two buttons in the transport, either side of the frame steps, and Option+Left and Option+Right go to the previous and next key of the selected nodes, from the Viewer, Timeline, Dope Sheet or Curve Editor. Hover an animated row in Properties and two small arrows beside its key diamond jump between that control's own keys. Both stop playback, never move past the first or last key, and are dim where there is no key that way.
  • View selected: the eye on the Node Graph's toolbar (also in Settings > Node Graph) shows whichever node you select in the Viewer, as pressing 1 would. Turning it on or off isn't an undo step.
  • Touching two nodes links them: drop a node so its tile touches another and the one above feeds the one below, where that input is free (an existing wire is never replaced). One undo puts them back in their chain and where they were.
  • Move nodes below to fit (Settings > Node Graph, and the graph's Arrange menu): nodes below move down to make room for a node put in between two, and move up to close the gap a deleted node leaves, unless another node sits level with it.
  • Open and Save windows take a typed or pasted path: click the path bar, press Cmd-L or Shift-Cmd-G, or paste or type a path starting with / or ~. Return opens the folder, or the file; Esc puts the folders back.
  • The Kura Write has a matte task for color-grade mattes. It renders to renders/matte with alpha, as PNG 8-bit written raw (no color transform, so a full matte stays 1 in every channel); 16-bit and EXR (ACEScg) are still available. Comps saved before keep their task.
  • Projection has guided steps: on Simple it shows six steps (Use, Picture, Hold, Surface, Check, Finish), with only the current step's rows showing and All controls one click away.   • SmartMerge has an Edge section: soften and choke (or grow) A's matte edge before it goes over, so an element doesn't look cut out.   • Furea's lens picker: the lens row opens a picker in place of the long lens menu. Each design is drawn in section with a ghost's path; studio lenses are listed by maker, with a zoom shown once with its measured focals; plus imported .lens files, Find, and the focal as chips.
  • Furea bends by the lens's distortion: choose a studio lens and set bend by its distortion (0 to 1, off by default) to curve the flare's ghosts, streak and glow by that lens's measured distortion. Each light's core stays on its light, and comps saved before render as they did.
  • Furea: every element has its own glow, with glow intensity and glow spread rows in its section. The anamorphic's soft cyan bloom round the light is now the Core's glow, the streak's halo and faint band are the Horizontal streak's glow, and any other element can take a soft glow of its own (none until you raise it). Flares and comps you already have render exactly as before.

Improved

  • ColorLookup, HueCorrect and HSVTool show the picture behind their graphs and take picks from the Viewer: ColorLookup is drawn in stops (its own 0 to 1 a click away) with the picture's brightness behind; HueCorrect shows the picture's hues behind a hue strip in degrees; Key from Viewer marks where the pixel under the pointer sits on the curve and keys it with a click; the target eyedropper reads what the Viewer shows. Keys you add take slopes that never overshoot, written so Nuke draws the same curve, and HueCorrect keeps 0 and 6 one value. HSVTool's Source from Viewer sets its ranges round the color you click and Target from Viewer the change to another; its hue range is drawn as a band over the picture's hues. What these nodes write is still what Nuke reads.
  • Viewers check whether they're on screen only when something changes (a tab, a window, a divider dragged, Kento coming forward), plus once a second, instead of four times a second each and on every redraw. That frees Python for the render threads while a comp works out its frames.
  • Painted slider tracks: a color control shows what it does before you touch it. The colors, and every color row's swatch, are shown through the comp's Viewer display, so they match the picture whatever the comp's color space.
